title: [Bug]: Pipeline Parallelism scheduler does not split sequences into pipeline micro-batches
body:
### Your current environment



### Environment

- Hardware: NVIDIA GB300 (SM103) NVL72
- Model: DeepSeek-R1-0528-FP4
- Workload: ISL = 128K, OSL = 1, aggregated mode, single 4-GPU node


### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

Under `pipeline-parallel-size > 1`, the vLLM scheduler dispatches up to `max_running_seq` sequences at once to the first pipeline stage instead of splitting them into `max_running_seq / PP_size` micro-batches per stage. As a result, enabling chunked prefill under PP adds scheduling and kernel-launch overhead **without** activating pipeline parallelism — chunks are serialized rather than pipelined.

### Environment

- Hardware: NVIDIA GB300 (SM103) NVL72
- Model: DeepSeek-R1-0528-FP4
- Workload: ISL = 128K, OSL = 1, aggregated mode, single 4-GPU node

### Reproduction

Configuration: `--pipeline-parallel-size 4 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens <chunk>`. Sweep `<chunk>` over {4K, 12K, 32K} and compare against no-chunk baseline. All other knobs identical.

### Observed behavior — chunk-size sweep on GB300, PP4, ISL=128K / OSL=1

| Config         | Peak TPS/GPU |
|----------------|:------------:|
| No-chunk       |   **1,678**  |
| Chunk 32K      |    ~1,500    |
| Chunk 12K      |    1,536     |
| Chunk 4K       |    1,347     |

Under correctly pipelined micro batching, more chunks per request should produce **more** pipeline fill and **higher** throughput (4K > 12K > 32K > no-chunk). We observe the **opposite** ordering: smaller chunks are strictly worse, and every chunked configuration loses the concurrency scaling that the no-chunk baseline has.

this is the empirical signature of chunks being serialized through the pipeline rather than flowing through stages as micro-batches.

### Root cause (from internal code review)

In the PP scheduler path, the running set is dispatched in a single batch up to `max_running_seq` sequences, sent to the first pipeline stage. There is no splitting into `max_running_seq / PP_size` micro-batches across stages, so the remaining stages are starved instead of overlapped.


### Related issues

- [#40674](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40674) — PP + `NixlConnector` for disaggregated serving.
- Companion RFC: long-context-optimized PP (CPP + Async P2P + Dynamic Chunking), see SGLang's [chunked-pipeline blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-01-15-chunked-pipeline/) for the design these features should align with.

title: [RFC]: Long-context-optimized Pipeline Parallelism, CPP + Async P2P + Dynamic Chunking
body:
### Your current environment

### Motivation

vLLM's current Pipeline Parallelism implementation is positioned in the [official docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/serving/parallelism_scaling/) as a *capacity or memory* fallback:

> *"Multi-node multi-GPU using tensor parallel and pipeline parallel inference: if the model is too large for a single node, combine tensor parallelism with pipeline parallelism."*

This positioning is correct for the original PP use case, but it leaves a sizable performance opportunity on the table for **long-context disaggregated serving**, where PP on the prefill side is the right tool to (a) compress the prefill pool (fewer prefill GPUs feeding the same number of decode GPUs) and (b) hide long-context attention bubbles via micro-batched stages.

[SGLang's chunked-pipeline blog (2026-01-15)](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-01-15-chunked-pipeline/) demonstrates that long-context PP needs a specific *combination* of three techniques to actually win. Reference numbers (DeepSeek-V3.1 on H20):

- **PP4 TP8 with DCK 12K → 3.31× prefill throughput** over the TP8 baseline.
- At matched GPU count (32 GPUs), **PP4 TP8 outperforms PP1 TP32 by 30.5%** with DCK, and still by 18.4% even with fixed 12K chunks — i.e. the architectural advantage is not just from dynamic chunking.
- **Strong-scaling efficiency at PP4: 82.8%** — the bubble overhead is effectively absorbed once `M ≫ P`.

vLLM today has **none** of the three pieces SGLang relies on. As a result, in our own measurements on GB300 NVL72 (DeepSeek-R1-0528-FP4, ISL=128K / OSL=1, aggregated), PP4 + chunked prefill (1,536 TPS/GPU) is *slower* than PP4 with no chunking (1,678 TPS/GPU), because the existing chunked-prefill path was designed for TP-only continuous batching ([SARATHI](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.16369), [DeepSpeed-FastGen Dynamic SplitFuse](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.08671)) and does not address PP bubble reduction.


### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Proposed feature

Add a long-context-optimized PP path with the following three components, gated behind an opt-in flag (e.g. `--pipeline-parallel-mode long-context`):

1. **Chunked Pipeline Parallelism (CPP)** — split a *single* long prompt into pipeline micro-batches that flow concurrently through stages. This is distinct from vLLM's existing chunked prefill (which targets *inter-request* decode piggybacking).
2. **Asynchronous P2P** — overlap GPU computation with stage-to-stage p2p transfers to reduce idle bubbles (today's PP path serializes compute with P2P).
3. **Dynamic Chunking (DCK)** — choose chunk size as a function of the per-request prefix length so attention runtime is roughly uniform across stages, minimizing bubbles caused by quadratic attention.

### Companion / pre-requisite

- [#40674](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40674) — PP + `NixlConnector` for disaggregated serving. Long-context PP is most useful on the prefill side of disagg deployments, which today cannot use PP because of the connector gap. This RFC assumes #40674 lands first or in parallel.

### Use case / context

- Model: DeepSeek-R1 (FP4) on Blackwell (GB300 NVL72), ISL=128K / OSL=8K, disaggregated.
- Goal: shrink the prefill pool via PP on prefill workers (matching the deployment pattern already validated by SGLang on the same model class) while keeping decode on TP / DP+EP. Prefill-pool compression is the largest single architectural-level gap we observe between vLLM and SGLang on GB300 long-context.

title: [Performance]: RMSNorm op in v0.20 IR layer prevent further pytorch/triton op fusion
body:
### Proposal to improve performance N/A ### Report of performance regression This is discovered when vLLM-Omni uses vllm's RMSNorm op and observes a performance regression. All discussion below assumes torch compile is enabled and the platform is H200 with CUDA platform ## Background/Our downstream analysis & setup - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/3266 - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/pull/3352
Reproduceable example (based on the links above) Set up vllm and vllm omni ``` uv venv -p 3.12 . .venv/bin/activate uv pip install vllm==0.20.0 --torch-backend=cu130 git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni.git cd vllm-omni uv pip install -e '.[dev]' ``` Run text-to-image generation with profiling, on main ``` python examples/offline_inference/text_to_image/text_to_image.py --model Qwen/Qwen-Image --prompt 'Random prompt 1 for benchmarking diffusion models' --negative-prompt 'Negative prompt 1 for benchmarking diffusion models' --width 1536 --height 1536 --num-inference-steps 3 --profiler-config '{ "profiler": "torch", "torch_profiler_dir": "./profiler-0.20.0-cu130", "torch_profiler_with_stack": true, "torch_profiler_use_gzip": true, "torch_profiler_record_shapes": true }' ``` Run the same profiling on v0.19 ``` # in vllm-omni folder git checkout dd0fa02547aae9f57e1cb1c80b7db50a4161b8d2 uv venv .19 -p 3.12 . .19/bin/activate uv pip install vllm==0.19.0 --torch-backend=cu129 uv pip install -e '.[dev]' ``` Run the same profiling with `vllm_c` setting even if torch.compile is on. ``` cd .. git clone -b fix-qwen-image-perf-1 https://github.com/fhfuih/vllm-omni.git vllm-omni-patch cd vllm-omni-patch uv venv -p 3.12 . .venv/bin/activate uv pip install vllm==0.20.0 --torch-backend=cu130 git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni.git cd vllm-omni uv pip install -e '.[dev]' ```
## TLDR In vllm v0.19 (with torch 2.10 and CUDA 12.9), RMSNorm becomes several native ops in torch Dynamo output, which further gets fused into a torch inductor. In vllm v0.20 (with torch 2.11 and CUDA 13.0), RMSNorm is seemingly wrapped in one atomic torch op, preventing torch to later fusing it no matter what. ## Suggestion 1 When VLLM IR set `ir_op_priority` to `native`, it wraps up those unfused native ops, potentially making torch inductor fail to fuse it, leading to ~15%-20% performance regression. CUDA graphs below: **vllm v0.19** **vllm v0.20, with `ir_op_priority` set to `native`** (The huge pink block above corresponds to the flagged area) Since this is "the platform defaults (when compiling with Inductor)", I assume the expected behavior is to "not fuse on vLLM's side" and "let torch inductor optimize it". So the current behavior goes against it. ## Suggestion 2 (lower priority, IDK if it is intended) When VLLM IR set `ir_op_priority` to `vllm_c`, the vllm-version of the fused op is slightly lower than the torch inductor's version **vllm v0.19 (again)** ~64us **vllm v0.20, with `ir_op_priority` set to `vllm_c`** ~83us I don't know if this is intended or the best we can get. But since the "native" version has performance degradation, we have to compare the `vllm_c` performance and the "old native" performance in production. ### Misc discussion on performance _No response_ ### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary) ```text The output of `python collect_env.py` ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Bug]: an unclosed <tool_call> opener written in prose holds the Qwen3 parser in tool state and swallows a later genuine tool call
body:
**Environment.** As in A (Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4, vLLM 0.28.0, `qwen3_coder`, template sha256 `0a20a467…abab9ab`).

**Describe the bug.** When the model mentions `<tool_call>` in prose without closing it — common when it explains or demonstrates the tool-call format — the state machine stays in tool state. Everything after is consumed as that span's body, including `</think>` and including a subsequent genuine tool call, which is therefore never emitted. The client receives a call named after the *first*, quoted block and does not receive the real one.

**Frequency.** 131 of 3,600 generations (3.6%) in our suite contain unbalanced `<tool_call>` markup (openers ≠ closers); 119 of those come from a prompt that asks the model to show the markup. At least one loses a genuine call as described.

**Concrete instance.** One generation, character offsets into the decoded output:

```
 2470  <tool_call>            <- opener, never closed
 2482  <function=function_name
 2890  <tool_call>            <- second opener, never closed
 4493  </think>
 4503  <tool_call>
 4515  <function=get_weather  <- the genuine call
 4586  </tool_call>           <- closes the span opened at 2470
```

The server returned `['function_name', 'get_weather', 'function_name']`; the final `function_name` is the span opened at 2,470 and closed at 4,586, and the real `get_weather` at 4,503 is inside its body. Replaying this through `Qwen3Parser` reproduces it exactly.

**Why the adjacent work does not cover it.** #56658 / #56661 add a function-header check before committing a span; this span *has* a header (`<function=function_name`), so that check confirms it rather than rejecting it. #50986 (`validate_tool_names`) drops the outer span because `function_name` is not offered — but the genuine call is inside that span's body and is dropped with it. Neither recovers the lost call.

**Suggested direction.** Bound how far a tool span may run — a turn-boundary or `</think>` token inside an open span is strong evidence the opener was prose, not markup — or reconsider the span at `finish()` when it never closed lexically. Raw generations available.

AI assistance was used for the investigation and the measurement harness; I reviewed the findings and ran everything described here on my own hardware.

title: [RFC]: Hardening /v1/messages (Anthropic API) for Claude Code across model families
body:
### Motivation

Claude Code can run against vLLM through the Anthropic Messages endpoint (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` → `/v1/messages`). Claude Code's agentic loop is a demanding client of that endpoint:

- It sends every request with ~25 tools, many with large nested JSON schemas.
- It uses interleaved thinking with parallel tool calls.
- It sends inline `role: "system"` messages that change every turn.
- It sends side queries (title generation, the auto-mode permission classifier) with `stop_sequences` and small `max_tokens` budgets.
- It recovers from context overflow based on the error it gets back.

This issue audits the current converter (`vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/`) and the HF chat templates of the major open model families against real Claude Code traffic. We found:

- several gaps that affect every model family;
- a set of model-specific breakages, some of which return **400 on Claude Code's default requests**.

Many of the small fixes already have open PRs, often more than one per problem. This issue gathers them so they can be deduplicated and prioritized, and it proposes the pieces that have no owner yet.

**How we checked**

- We captured `/v1/messages` traffic from Claude Code 2.1.281 through a logging proxy (~50 requests covering main-loop turns, title generation and the auto-mode classifier).
- We replayed synthetic Claude Code-shaped conversations through `AnthropicServingMessages.to_chat_completion_request` → `chat_utils` post-processing.
- We rendered the result with the current HF templates, and with `mistral_common` / the DeepSeek Python encoders / Harmony where applicable.

Items marked *(unverified)* were not reproduced at runtime.

**Observed request shape (from captures)**

| Field | Values seen |
|---|---|
| `system` | List of text blocks with `cache_control`. The first is the `x-anthropic-billing-header` line. |
| `messages` | Contains inline `role: "system"` messages at non-leading positions (e.g. a `<total_tokens>` update each turn). |
| `thinking` | `{"type":"adaptive"}`, `{"type":"adaptive","display":"omitted"}`, `{"type":"enabled"}`, `{"type":"disabled"}`, or absent |
| `output_config` | `{"effort":"high"}`; title generation adds `format: json_schema` |
| `context_management` | `{"edits":[{"type":"clear_thinking_20251015","keep":"all"}]}` |
| `max_tokens` | `32000` (main loop), `2112` (classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</block>"]`), `64` (stage-1 classifier, `stop_sequences: ["</severity>"]`) |
| `tool_result` | `is_error` is set on most results. Content is a string or a list of text/image blocks. User turns often carry extra text blocks (system reminders) after the tool results. |

---

### Part 1: Converter / API gaps (all models)

| # | Gap | Location | Impact | Existing work |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Inline system messages are always hoisted into the leading system prompt.** `_detect_merge_inline_system` is called with the CLI `--chat-template` value, which is `None` by default, so it returns `True` for every deployment that uses the model's own template. Claude Code sends a changing inline system message every turn, so the leading system text changes every request. | `serving.py:142,152,248-257` | **Prefix cache misses on the whole conversation, every turn.** Also changes semantics: mid-conversation instructions become part of the global system prompt. | #53393, #48874, #41114, #46710; PRs #53501, #56520, #52978, #47681 (competing approaches) |
| 2 | **The `thinking` request field is silently dropped.** `AnthropicMessagesRequest` has no `thinking` field and pydantic ignores extras. `output_config.effort` → `reasoning_effort` then forces `enable_thinking=True` (`chat_completion/protocol.py:585`). Anthropic's default when `thinking` is absent is *off*, but we use the template default, which is usually *on*. | `protocol.py:121` | Side queries (title generation, classifier) reason and spend their `max_tokens` budget before answering. `display: "omitted"` is ignored. | PRs #58613, #53058 |
| 3 | **Stop strings are matched against reasoning text.** `check_stop_strings` runs over the full detokenized output. | `v1/engine/detokenizer.py:130` | The classifier's `</block>` / `</severity>` can match inside `<think>` and end the request with no verdict. | #51669 (related) |
| 4 | **Context-overflow errors are not in Anthropic's format.** vLLM returns "This model's maximum context length is …". Claude Code decides whether to auto-compact or retry with a smaller `max_tokens` based on Anthropic's context-limit error messages *(exact strings unverified)*. Claude Code always sends `max_tokens=32000`, so a 128k-context deployment rejects prompts once they pass ~99k tokens. | `renderers/params.py:357,499` | Long sessions fail hard instead of compacting. | none found |
| 5 | **Unknown content-block types reject the whole request (422).** `AnthropicContentBlock.type` is a closed `Literal`. `document` (PDFs from the Read tool), `search_result`, `tool_addition` / `tool_removal` and server-tool blocks all fail. Once one is in the history, every later request in the session fails. | `protocol.py:41` | Session becomes unrecoverable. | #57324, #46790; PRs #45653, #57693, #46797, #47747, #47877 |
| 6 | **Images in a `tool_result` become a separate `user` message** inserted between tool messages. | `serving.py:445-455` | Gemma 4 silently drops later tool results. Mistral returns 400 (`Unexpected role 'tool' after role 'user'`). DeepSeek-V3.2 raises. MiniMax-M3 and Gemma 4 could render the image inside the tool message natively. | none found |
| 7 | **`tool_reference` produces an extra tool message, and the first one is empty.** | `serving.py:457-465` | 400 on Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 (`Unexpected item type in content`) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (`No tool calls but found tool output`). Python repr rendered on MiniMax. | #52489; PRs #52498, #52610 |
| 8 | **User text after `tool_result`s in the same turn becomes a separate trailing `user` message.** Templates that keep reasoning only after the last user message then drop the current tool loop's reasoning. | `serving.py:306` | Interleaved thinking lost mid-loop on GLM-4.7/5/5.1/5.2, Qwen3.5/3.6, MiniMax-M2.x and DeepSeek-V3.2. | none found |
| 9 | **`is_error` on `tool_result` is dropped.** | `serving.py:408-445` | The model cannot tell failed tool calls from successful ones. | none found |
| 10 | **System blocks are joined with `""`.** | `serving.py:257` | Prompt text runs together, e.g. `…for Claude.You are…`. | none found |
| 11 | **Malformed tool-call arguments crash non-streaming** (`json.loads` → 500). | `serving.py` (`messages_full_converter`) | Hard failure on a single bad generation. | PRs #57244, #52519 |
| 12 | **Error envelopes and types don't match Anthropic's.** FastAPI 422s are not wrapped in Anthropic's error format. Stream errors use `internal_error` instead of `api_error` / `overloaded_error`. Mid-stream upstream errors are replaced with "Invalid data format received". | `api_router.py`, `serving.py` | Client retry/backoff logic doesn't fire correctly. | PRs #58023, #46162 |
| 13 | **`x-api-key` is not accepted** by `--api-key` auth. | `serve/middleware/authenticate.py` | Requires `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` instead of `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. | PRs #51675, #51588 |
| 14 | **No `ping` or early `message_start` during long prefills** (100k+ token prompts). | `serving.py` (`message_stream_converter`) | Idle-timeout risk through proxies and load balancers *(unverified)*. | none found |
| 15 | **Tool-call id collisions/format.** vLLM-generated ids are reused across turns for some parsers (e.g. Kimi `functions.X:0`). | | See Kimi below. | PR #35667 |

---

### Part 2: Model / template-specific findings

The common thread: every family uses **different names and values** for thinking and effort. Examples: `enable_thinking`, `thinking`, `thinking_mode`, `low_effort`, `thinking_budget`, and effort sets such as `{low,high}`, `{none,high}` or `{xhigh,medium,low}`. Passing `output_config.effort` straight through as `reasoning_effort` therefore gives inconsistent behavior, and 400s on several families.

| Family | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3.8** (27B, Flash-Next, 2.4T) | The template raises `Unexpected reasoning effort high. Supported types are xhigh (default), medium, and low.` Claude Code sends `high` by default, so **every default Claude Code request returns 400**. 2.4T also raises `Disabling thinking is not supported.` | confirmed |
| **Qwen3.5 / 3.6** | Keep reasoning only after the last user message (item 8). 3.6 supports `preserve_thinking`, which vLLM never sets. The system-first guard is hidden only by item 1. | confirmed |
| **Qwen3.5 / Qwen3-Coder** | Historical arguments rendered with `\| string` produce Python `True`. Qwen3-Coder renders nested `anyOf` lossily. | confirmed (template-side) |
| **GLM-5.2 / 5.3** | Effort is mapped as `'high' if effort == 'high' else 'max'` (5.2), or only `{low,high}` is recognized (5.3), so `low`/`medium` become **Max**. 5.3 cannot disable thinking: the generation prompt is always `<think>`. `glm47_moe` parser switches to content-only when `enable_thinking=False`, so a naive disabled-thinking mapping would leak reasoning into `content`. | confirmed |
| **MiniMax-M3** | The template's `thinking_mode` (`enabled`/`disabled`/`adaptive`) maps 1:1 to Anthropic `thinking.type`, but vLLM never sets it. The template has no branch for non-leading system messages, so they are silently dropped once item 1 is fixed. | confirmed |
| **MiniMax-M2.x** | Reasoning is dropped before the last user message (item 8). | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V3.1** | The stock HF template does `'<｜tool▁sep｜>' + arguments`, but `chat_utils` has already turned arguments into a dict, so rendering raises `TypeError` on any history containing a tool call. It also never renders `tools`. Workaround: `examples/tool_chat_template_deepseekv31.jinja`. | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V3.2** (encoder) | `drop_thinking = messages[-1]["role"] == "user"` drops the current loop's reasoning (item 8). The strict tool-ordering check breaks on items 6 and 7. A non-merged inline system message has no role token and lands inside `<think>`. | confirmed |
| **DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1** | V4 is fine. V4.1 raises on `effort: "medium"` (accepts low/high/xhigh/max). | confirmed |
| **Kimi K2-Thinking / K2.5 / K2.6** | The template renders only the tool-call **id**, never the tool name (`<\|tool_call_begin\|>{{ id }}`). Any id not generated by Kimi on vLLM (`toolu_…`, `chatcmpl-tool-…`, after `/model` or a resumed session) loses the tool name. Thinking uses `thinking`, not `enable_thinking`. | confirmed |
| **Kimi K3** | Only low/high/max effort are accepted, so `medium` / `xhigh` return 400. Tool-result matching is robust to foreign ids. | confirmed |
| **gpt-oss (Harmony)** | `max` / `xhigh` effort raise. Reasoning cannot be disabled. Images are dropped. Each inline system message becomes a new developer message. JSON Schema → TypeScript is lossy: `anyOf`+enum, `allOf`, `$ref` and `const` become `any`, and `additionalProperties` maps become `{}` (affects Claude Code's `AskUserQuestion` / `Workflow` tools). | confirmed |
| **Mistral / Devstral** | `validate_request_params` allows only `{none, high}` effort, so Claude Code's other values return 400. Devstral-Small-2 and Devstral-2 raise `think tokens are not available for this tokenizer` whenever the history contains a thinking block. `truncate_tool_call_ids` works but logs a WARNING per historical tool call on every request. | confirmed |
| **Gemma 4** | Later tool results are lost when a user message is inserted (item 6). The template renders `anyOf` as an empty type, renders enums only for strings, and renders map-typed objects as fake properties (hits `AskUserQuestion`). | confirmed |
| **Nemotron v3** | The template reads `low_effort`, which vLLM never sets, so effort has no effect. Thinking cannot be disabled via the Anthropic API. | confirmed |
| **Seed-OSS** | Thinking is controlled only by `thinking_budget` (default unlimited). The default tool rendering is Python signatures that drop nested types and enums; `use_json_tooldef` fixes this but is off by default. Historical arguments use Python repr. | confirmed |

---

### Proposed Change

Suggested priority order:

1. **Per-model thinking/effort mapping layer.** Map Anthropic `thinking.type` (+ `budget_tokens`) and `output_config.effort` onto each model's native switch (`enable_thinking`, `thinking`, `thinking_mode`, `low_effort`, `thinking_budget`) and clamp to the levels that model accepts. Treat absent `thinking` as disabled only where the model can actually disable it. This extends #58613 and #52738, and removes most of the 400s above.
2. **Inline system handling that preserves the prefix.** Keep inline system messages in place, or fold them into the adjacent user turn when the template requires system-first (as proposed in #53393). Never hoist them into the leading system block. Detect the template requirement against the *resolved* tokenizer template, not the CLI flag.
3. **Converter structure fixes.**
   - Keep tool-result images inside the `tool` message.
   - Emit one merged user message per Anthropic user turn, so the trailing text doesn't cut off reasoning.
   - Mark `is_error` (e.g. an `Error:` prefix).
   - Join system blocks with `\n\n`.
   - Emit a single `tool_reference` message.
4. **Error compatibility.**
   - Translate context-overflow errors to Anthropic's messages so Claude Code can auto-compact or reduce `max_tokens`.
   - Degrade unknown content blocks to text instead of failing with 422.
   - Use Anthropic error types and envelopes throughout.
5. **Model-specific fixes.**
   - Rewrite Kimi tool-call ids to `functions.{name}:{idx}`.
   - Drop historical reasoning for Mistral tokenizers without `[THINK]`.
   - Add a schema-normalization pass (flatten `anyOf`/`$ref`) for Harmony, Gemma 4 and Seed-OSS.
   - Evaluate stop strings against content only, not reasoning.
6. **Regression coverage.** Add a small Claude Code-shaped fixture (captured request shapes, no user content) to `tests/entrypoints/anthropic/`, rendered through the converter for each supported template family.

### Feedback Period

~2 weeks.

### CC List

_No response_

### Any Other Things

AI assistance was used for this investigation (Claude Code): it analyzed the captured traffic, read the converter code and rendered templates across model families. File/line references are against `main` at e33de821c0.

title: [Question] Support path for platform plugins that cannot install Triton (MRV2 requires it)
body:
### Context

We maintain a platform plugin ([vllm-openvino](https://github.com/belonghim/vllm-openvino)) that replaces the Platform, Worker and Model Runner for an OpenVINO backend. OpenVINO is incompatible with `torch.compile`/Inductor, so the plugin cannot install Triton (its install docs require `pip uninstall -y triton`). The plugin's runner consumes `vllm.v1.worker.gpu_input_batch` (`InputBatch`, `CachedRequestState`) and builds its attention metadata directly from the scheduler output.

### Observation (v0.29.0)

- `VllmConfig.use_v2_model_runner` silently falls back to the V1 runner when Triton is absent — the plugin sees `Model Runner V2 requires Triton; using the V1 model runner instead.`
- `VllmConfig._validate_v2_model_runner` raises `ValueError("Model Runner V2 requires Triton.")` when V2 is requested explicitly.

So MRV2 is currently unreachable for backends that cannot ship Triton, and such backends stay on V1 runner internals.

### Questions

1. Is there a deprecation or removal plan for the V1 model runner / `vllm.v1.worker.gpu_input_batch`? If so, what support window should plugins that use those modules plan for?
2. Does the non-Triton work (e.g. #55847 CPU torch fallbacks, #45133 Triton kernel dispatcher, #51212 pluggable V2 design) intend to cover non-CPU plugins that replace the runner entirely, or should such backends plan to stop depending on runner internals?
3. If the latter, would a small documented interface for replacement runners be an acceptable contribution, instead of plugins importing from `v1/worker/*`?

We can test V2-related changes on CPU/OpenVINO and are happy to provide feedback or help.

title: [Bug]: Kimi-K3-NVFP4 on 8xB300 produces degenerate, incoherent output in the reasoning channel on v0.27.0
body:
### Your current environment

We are not able to run `collect_env.py` against the affected build. It was a production deployment that has since been rolled back, so that container no longer exists. The information below is therefore split into the node-level facts (identical across both builds, since it is the same physical machine) and the identity of the affected build.

**Node — unchanged between the working and the failing build**

| | |
|---|---|
| GPUs | 8x NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC (288 GB each), NV18 full mesh |
| NVIDIA driver | 595.71.05 |
| CUDA runtime | 13.0.88 |
| Host OS | Talos Linux (immutable, no host userland), kernel `6.18.34-talos` |
| Container userland | Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64), glibc 2.39, Python 3.12.3 — from the vLLM image |
| CPU | 224 vCPU, 2 NUMA nodes, KVM guest |

**Affected build:** the published `v0.27.0` release image (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.0`) — vLLM 0.27.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130, FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3, Triton 3.7.1,
transformers 5.15.0, as pinned for that tag.


### 🐛 Describe the bug

## What we run

`RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-NVFP4` served on a single node of 8x B300, tensor parallel 8, weights loaded. Serving flags:

```
--tensor-parallel-size=8
--gpu-memory-utilization=0.95
--max-model-len=262144
--max-num-batched-tokens=8192
--max-num-seqs=64
--kv-cache-dtype=fp8
--attention-config={"use_prefill_query_quantization":true,"mla_prefill_backend":"flashinfer"}
--enable-prefix-caching
--load-format=fastsafetensors
--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune
--trust-remote-code
--enable-auto-tool-choice
--tool-call-parser=kimi_k3
--reasoning-parser=kimi_k3
--enable-prompt-tokens-details
```

## What we observed

On `v0.27.0` the model produces degenerate, incoherent text in the reasoning channel. The prompt
was as simple as `hello how are you`. The reasoning content came back as:

```
G now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now now
{ how are now now now now now now
)
[ how are now }
[ are now now now now now now now now
 are now
[ is now now is now
[ G is now now is now now
 )
G is now
[ now now is now now now now now now now now now now now
= is now now
= now now is now
- is now
-G is now
- now now
- G now
-G is this
- this
- this
```

- **It appeared immediately, on a trivially short prompt.** This did not develop after hours of
  serving, under load, or after a long-context request. It was present essentially from the
  first request after the version change, with a prompt of five words.

- **Nothing crashed or reported an error.** No CUDA errors, no illegal memory access, no
  assertion failures, no NaN-related aborts, no engine restarts. The pod stayed `Running` with 0
  restarts and kept answering requests at normal latency. The failure was completely silent from
  an operational standpoint: health checks and metrics looked entirely normal while the output
  was garbage. That is the part we found most concerning — nothing in our monitoring would have
  caught this.

## What changed to trigger it

We had been serving this model on a **nightly build from 2026-08-09** without this symptom. We
then moved the deployment to the **`v0.27.0` release tag** and changed nothing else — same
physical node, same GPUs, same driver, same weights, same flags. The degenerate output appeared
with that change. As mitigation we rolled the deployment back to that same nightly.

We want to be precise about the limits of this evidence: we changed builds, we did not bisect
individual commits, so we cannot point at a specific change as the cause. What we can say is
that the `v0.27.0` release tag shows it on this configuration and a nightly from a few days
before the release did not. Kimi-K3 support is very new and appears to be changing quickly, so
we wondered whether the release branch is simply missing model fixes that landed on `main`
shortly before the tag was cut — but that is speculation on our part, and someone with a view of
what went into the branch is far better placed to judge it than we are.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Bug]: --load_format fastsafetensors produces corrupted/incoherent generation for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 with TP+EP (works with default loader)
body:
### Your current environment

- **Hardware**: 2× NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), one GPU per node, 2-node cluster joined via Ray (TCP/RoCE interconnect)
- **Compute Capability**: SM121 (12.1), `aarch64`
- **vLLM**: 0.26.0 (PyPI release)
- **torch**: 2.11.0+cu130
- **CUDA**: 13.0
- **Distributed executor**: `ray`, `--tensor-parallel-size 2` (one GPU per node), `--enable-expert-parallel`

### Model

```
deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `--load_format fastsafetensors`, the server starts and serves requests without error, but generation output is incoherent (not just low-quality — literal token salad mixing unrelated languages/scripts/digits), **even under greedy decoding (`temperature=0`)**. Switching to the default loader (removing the flag entirely) with an otherwise-identical launch command produces fluent, well-formed text for the same prompt and sampling parameters.

This looks like a weight-loading correctness bug specific to `fastsafetensors` for this model's TP+EP sharding, not a config or template issue — we independently ruled out chat-template/prompt-encoding as the cause (verified via `/tokenize` that the prompt's special tokens resolve to the exact expected IDs), and ruled out sampling randomness (reproduced identically at `temperature=0`).

### Launch command (bugged)

```bash
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --distributed-executor-backend ray \
  --load_format fastsafetensors \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --block-size 256 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8
```

### Repro

Prompt (raw `/v1/completions`, DeepSeek-V4's own chat-mode encoding, `add_special_tokens=false`):
```
<｜begin▁of▁sentence｜><｜User｜>What is 2+2? Answer in one word.<｜Assistant｜></think>
```

**With `--load_format fastsafetensors`** (`temperature=1.0`, `max_tokens=32`):
```
eBook '++lang()' non e 'undefined'.
        // In quel caso non deve essere tradotto.
        // Nota: menzionare un OG
```

**Without `--load_format fastsafetensors`** (identical prompt/params, only the loader changed):
```
eBook. Please don't try to read it directly.","price":0,"duration":0,"currency":null,"url":"https://www.smashwords.com/books/view/860089"}]...
```
(Still doesn't answer the question — that's a separate, likely attention/kernel-level issue we're still isolating — but the text is grammatically well-formed English/JSON rather than token salad.)

### Expected behavior

Output coherence (grammaticality) should not depend on the weight-loading backend used, given both claim to load the same checkpoint bit-for-bit. This suggests `fastsafetensors` is either mis-mapping tensors (e.g. quantization scale tensors paired with the wrong weight tensor) or mis-sharding weights for this model's TP+EP configuration.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the documentation page, which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

Container image is a community build (`ghcr.io/spark-arena/dgx-vllm-eugr-nightly`), but the affected code is stock `vllm` under `/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/vllm/`, not anything the image itself patches. ### 🐛 Describe the bug The Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint crashes whenever a client sends a `tool_result` content block whose `content` array includes an Anthropic `tool_reference` item. This happens organically with Claude Code sessions that have a large number of tools available (multiple MCP servers configured), where the Anthropic API's tool-search/dynamic-tool-discovery beta feature lets a tool result reference another tool by name instead of re-embedding its full definition. Once a `tool_reference` block appears anywhere in a conversation's history, every subsequent request in that conversation fails — the coding agent gets no further responses. **Root cause:** `_convert_user_tool_result` in [`vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py) converts every other known item type (`text`, `image`) into a template-safe OpenAI content item, but for `tool_reference` it appends the **raw, unconverted** Anthropic-shaped block instead: ```python elif item_type == "tool_reference": ref_name = item.get("tool_name") or item.get("name") if ref_name: tool_reference.append( {"type": "tool_reference", "name": ref_name} ) ... if tool_reference: openai_messages.append( { "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": block.tool_use_id or "", "content": tool_reference, # <-- raw Anthropic-shaped items, never converted } ) ``` That raw `{"type": "tool_reference", "name": ...}` dict is handed straight to the model's chat template as the `content` of a `tool`-role message. Most Jinja chat templates (including Qwen3's, confirmed here) only understand content items shaped like `{"type": "text", "text": ...}` or `{"type": "image"/"image_url", ...}`; anything else falls through to a catch-all `raise_exception(...)` branch, so the request fails regardless of which model is served. **Minimal reproduction** (isolates the chat-template layer directly — no server needed, just the model's own tokenizer, reproducing exactly the content shape vLLM's converter produces): ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer import traceback tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4") # This is exactly the shape vllm/entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py's # _convert_user_tool_result() produces for a tool_result block containing # a tool_reference item: the raw Anthropic-shaped dict is passed straight # through as OpenAI-style chat message content, unconverted. messages = [ {"role": "user", "content": "What tools do I have available?"}, { "role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "toolu_01abc123", "content": [ {"type": "tool_reference", "name": "some_mcp_tool"} ], }, ] try: tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) print("NO ERROR (unexpected)") except Exception: traceback.print_exc() ``` **Observed output** (run against the model on disk in this deployment): ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "/tmp/repro_template.py", line 22, in tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/transformers/tokenization_utils_base.py", line 3108, in apply_chat_template rendered_chat, generation_indices = render_jinja_template( ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/transformers/utils/chat_template_utils.py", line 581, in render_jinja_template rendered_chat = compiled_template.render( ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/jinja2/environment.py", line 1295, in render self.environment.handle_exception() File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/jinja2/environment.py", line 942, in handle_exception raise rewrite_traceback_stack(source=source) File "

title: [Performance]: Weight loading is slow on GB10 (DGX Spark): per-tensor H2D copies straight from safetensors mmap views
body:
### Report of performance regression

Not a regression; a platform-dependent cost in the default safetensors load path. Related work on other hardware: #49991 (ROCm) and #50794 (Ascend NPU).

**Summary.** On GB10, `param.copy_(loaded_weight)` from a CPU tensor backed by the checkpoint's file mmap costs ~7× more than the same copy from ordinary (anonymous) memory. The cost is paid per tensor, so it dominates weight loading for checkpoints with many small tensors. Per-expert MoE checkpoints are the main case.

Reading the tensors into anonymous memory before the copy (`clone()`, or `pread` into a fresh tensor) gives identical bytes and removes most of it.

**Micro-benchmark.** For each variant: copy every routed-expert weight (800 KiB NVFP4) and block scale (100 KiB) of one real 9 GiB shard to the GPU, one tensor at a time, as `RoutedExperts._load_w13` / `_load_w2` do. Each variant ran in a fresh process on a shard no earlier run touched, with the page cache dropped first. All variants produced byte-identical weights.

| variant | ms / tensor |
|---|---|
| A: mmap view → `param.copy_()` (current) | 1.74 |
| E: shard read into the page cache first, then A | 1.86–1.89 |
| F: `.clone()` the mmap view, then the same `copy_` | **0.23** |
| B: reused pinned bounce buffer | 0.22–0.26 |
| C: pinned staging per 3,072 tensors + GPU scatter | 0.25 |

E shows the page cache is not the issue: the copy is slow whenever its source is a file-backed page, resident or not. F shows a plain clone does as well as pinned staging. A native profile shows the time in `cuMemcpyHtoDAsync_v2` from pageable memory, with the CPU spinning in `libcuda`. I have not established why file-backed pages are slower than anonymous ones on this path. The likely place is the driver's pageable-copy handling on GB10's unified memory; #49991 found a related VMA-permission effect in KFD on ROCm.

**The read path, separately.** Reading one whole 9 GiB expert shard in the loader's order (`f.keys()`), CPU only, client page cache cold (checked with `mincore`), bytes identical:

| read path | time | throughput |
|---|---|---|
| mmap `get_tensor` + `.clone()` | 3.95–4.13 s | 2.2 GiB/s |
| `pread` each tensor into a fresh CPU tensor | 0.82 s | 10.9 GiB/s |

The checkpoint was on NFS over RDMA with the files in the server's RAM. mmap faults do not pipeline the way buffered reads with readahead do; that is an inference from these numbers, not a measurement of fault behavior.

**End to end.** `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` (512 experts, ~297k expert tensors), "Loading weights" for the main model, with out-of-tree patches:

| machine, base, weights on | stock | + clone in `_load_w13` / `_load_w2` | + `pread` in `safetensors_weights_iterator` (≤ 64 MiB) and 2 smaller fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spark 1, preview image, NFS over RDMA (server RAM) | 450–541 s (5 boots) | 150 s | 35.5 s |
| Spark 1, v0.30.0, local NVMe | not measured | 189.5 s | 97.4 / 99.5 s |
| Spark 2, v0.29.0, local NVMe | 452 s | 242 s | not measured |
| Spark 2, v0.30.0, local NVMe | not measured | 231 s | not measured |

Spark 2 is a different machine, measured by its owner. The last column also includes an indexed expert-name lookup (#58720) and chunked `embed_tokens` / `lm_head` copies, so it is not `pread` alone. Greedy outputs were identical between each patched and unpatched run.

### Proposal to improve performance

#49991 gates a clone on ROCm behind an env var. #50794 clones every tensor on Ascend. GB10 is a third platform with the same shape of problem. Rather than a third per-vendor switch, could the default iterator hand out anonymous-memory tensors when the destination is an accelerator? Options, cheapest first:

1. Clone before the H2D copy at the consumers (`RoutedExperts._load_w13` / `_load_w2`, linear `weight_loader`s, `VocabParallelEmbedding.weight_loader`). Local, but there are many call sites.
2. `pread` small tensors into fresh CPU tensors in `safetensors_weights_iterator` instead of yielding mmap views, keeping views above a size cap. This fixes every consumer at once and is also the faster read path above. The cost is one transient CPU tensor per yielded weight.
3. Make it a load strategy (`--safetensors-load-strategy`), default per platform.

For option 2, a size cap must keep very large tensors as views. Some models serve a table from the checkpoint by mmap at runtime and must not have it read into RAM; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 47.7 GiB PLE table is one (#54129, #58439).

Happy to put up a PR for whichever direction maintainers prefer. I didn't want to open a third per-platform PR next to #49991 and #50794.

### Your current environment

```text
DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory), aarch64, kernel 7.0.0-1019-nvidia, driver 580.178.04
vllm 0.30.0 (vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0), torch 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0), safetensors 0.8.0
```

AI assistance (Claude) was used for the profiling, the benchmarks and this write-up. I reviewed it and ran the measurements.

title: [Question][ROCm] GLM-5.3-Flash kpool indexer: does the 640-token block table reach 32-pool pages on gfx942/gfx950 too?
body:
We found this on hardware vLLM doesn't support (gfx1030, Radeon Pro V620), running GLM-5.3-Flash without aiter. The code path involved is shared with gfx942/gfx950, and we have no MI300/MI355 to check it on. Could someone with one confirm or rule it out?

**What we see.** `Glm5NextIndexerCache` stores pooled keys in pages of 32 pools (storage block 128 tokens at `index_kpool=4`). The hybrid KDA page rule makes the attention block 640. On ROCm the sparse-MLA and indexer backends accept `MultipleOf(16)` (`get_supported_kernel_block_sizes`), so `select_common_block_size` keeps kernel block 640. The indexer metadata builder only converts the table when the storage block is a multiple of the kernel block (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py`, prefill and decode branches; unchanged on main):

```python
if (
    kernel_block_size is not None
    and self.kv_cache_spec.block_size != kernel_block_size
    and self.kv_cache_spec.block_size % kernel_block_size == 0
):
    factor = self.kv_cache_spec.block_size // kernel_block_size
    indexer_block_table = (block_table[:, ::factor] // factor).contiguous()
```

128 % 640 ≠ 0, so the 640-token table goes to `get_compressed_slot_mapping` (the kpool writer) and to `cp_gather_indexer_k_quant_cache_triton` as if each entry named one 32-pool page. With per-chunk block allocation:
- pools written before their block exists land in padding;
- positions past the allocated blocks alias block 0;
- positions past the 52-column table (at `max_model_len` 32768) are masked by the gather.

On NVIDIA the kernel block is 64, so the `// factor` branch applies. As far as we can tell nothing here is aiter-specific: the kpool path uses `forward_cuda` on ROCm whether aiter is on or off.

**Reproducer.** One GPU, stock vLLM only, no model: [`repro_rocm_kpool_table.py`](https://github.com/Omnicef/vllm/blob/glm53-v030/tests/local/repro_rocm_kpool_table.py). It writes a 9,432-token prompt in the served prefill chunks with the real ROCm kpool writer and slot mapping, gathers it back with the real gather, and compares against the writer's own output. The two arms are the table as the builder produces it and a page-granular table (block `b` → pages `5b … 5b+4`). On gfx1030, identical over two runs:

```
table as the builder produces it  : ooo000000000000xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmmm  (3/74 pages correct)
page-granular table               : oooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo  (74/74 pages correct)
```

(`o` correct, `0` all-zero, `x` wrong keys, `m` masked.) Above `index_topk`, where the indexer actually selects, this breaks long-context retrieval: a two-fact needle at ~9k tokens failed for us until the table was expanded. If it reproduces on MI300, the fix we use expands each kernel-block id into its storage pages when the kernel block is a multiple of the storage block (about 20 lines in the builder, happy to send).

**Secondary note (tile order).** With aiter off (`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER` unset), the decode logits fall back to `fp8_paged_mqa_logits_torch`. It reads each page token-major, while two ROCm writers store values in 16×16 tiles when `block_size > 1`: `indexer_k_quant_and_cache_triton` and the GLM-5.3 kpool writer. DeepSeek-V4's C4A compressor (`compress_norm_rope_store_triton`) writes token-major, so its pages are unaffected. See the correction on #51555 for numbers. aiter's reader passes `Preshuffle=block_size > 1` and isn't affected.

title: [Performance]: Suboptimal SM90 FP8 CUTLASS MoE dispatch on H20 EP8 — upstream fix proposed
body:
### Current serving results (replaces older serving snapshots)

Three GuideLLM 0.7.4 runs per tier, 10 s warmup, separate 8xH20 nodes. Humming W4A8 on original MXFP4: Decode c256 4,725 ± 66 output tok/s; fixed-1K Prefill c64 9,875 ± 63 input tok/s. Tuned FP8-128 + flashinfer_cutlass: 6,459 ± 173 output tok/s (+36.7%) and 15,048 ± 818 input tok/s (+52.4%), respectively. Values are means ± sample standard deviations. Paired GSM8K: Humming 476/494 correct, tuned 475/494; one-question difference (0.20 percentage points). The [blog PR #350](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-project.github.io/pull/350) has per-run data and methods. These whole-recipe gains are not attributable to the FlashInfer patch alone; the isolated operator A/B below remains its direct evidence. AI assistance was used to prepare this update.

### Proposal to improve performance

Track an upstream FlashInfer dispatch optimization affecting vLLM's SM90 block-FP8 `flashinfer_cutlass` MoE path, and validate its integration once a release containing the fix is available.

Upstream implementation and reproduction script: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5560 (open, not yet merged).

The FlashInfer grouped GEMM runner uses the unexpanded input token count as `expected_m_`, but the dispatch threshold and tile selection operate on rows per expert. On our H20 EP8 configuration, a 288-token input with top-k=6 and 400 physical experts has an average of 4.32 routed rows per physical expert, not 288. The mismatched estimate selects an unfavorable GEMM branch/tile for decode-sized batches.

The proposed fix configures `max(1, ceil(tokens * top_k / (local_experts * ep_size)))` after worst-case workspace sizing. It keeps workspace virtual signatures, allocation logic and existing kernels unchanged. EPLB replicas are physical execution slots; this remains an average-load heuristic, not a measured routing histogram.

vLLM already forwards `ep_size`, `ep_rank` and `use_deepseek_fp8_block_scale` to FlashInfer. We are not proposing a duplicate dispatch implementation or LD_PRELOAD workaround in vLLM. The requested follow-up is dependency uptake and integration/performance validation after the upstream fix is reviewed and released.

### Report of performance regression

This is a suboptimal-dispatch report, **not a bisected vLLM release regression**.

Actual source-built comparison on eight H20 ranks, using the full local `cutlass_fused_moe` API:

| Input tokens / routing | Baseline ms | Proposed fix ms | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 192 / uniform | 1.796432 | 0.554240 | 3.24x |
| 288 / uniform | 1.808480 | 0.564064 | 3.21x |
| 2048 / uniform | 1.904528 | 0.720464 | 2.64x |
| 288 / 75% routed to six experts | 2.020800 | 1.018144 | 1.98x |
| 288 / six active experts, seven ranks empty | 0.791280 | 0.751328 | 1.05x |
| 1 / uniform | 0.114720 | 0.115152 | ~1.00x |
| Draft geometry, 288 / uniform | 0.633360 | 0.217456 | 2.91x |

Five warmups, 24 CUDA Graph/event samples, explicit 64 MiB L2 flush outside timing; median of per-sample maximum latency across eight ranks. CUPTI was unavailable and GPU clocks were not locked. Cross-rank output reduction was checked **outside** the timed region.

All 64 rank/case output comparisons (including two draft cases) had maximum absolute difference zero; combined outputs also passed. No LD_PRELOAD was used for these source-build results.

**These are local MoE operator measurements, not communication-inclusive latency or serving TPS. We do not claim a 3.21x end-to-end vLLM throughput improvement.**

### Misc discussion on performance

Reproduction: the upstream PR includes the eight-rank synthetic `full_moe.py` harness, build isolation instructions and baseline/candidate commands. It does not require access to our checkpoint. Run the baseline before the candidate to generate identical-input reference tensors.

Validation boundaries:

- The full extension compiled, linked and loaded from an isolated FlashInfer 0.6.18.post1 source copy with the patch backported. The measured baseline retains EP-argument plumbing from an earlier iteration but restores the original estimate; it is a controlled ablation, not a pristine upstream binary.
- Exact upstream-base build and unmodified pytest execution remain pending. The proposed upstream base is `bf82326b0c524048c7f810da9f0022f8316ac3ff`.
- EP8 sequential-shard reference checks passed at hidden/intermediate=128 with batch 512 → 192 → 1 → 288 and unchanged tolerance. These are distinct from the real eight-rank A/B checks above.
- A hidden=512/intermediate=256 independent-reference case failed identically on baseline and patch (5,330/262,144 elements). Its cause is not fully established; this is not recorded as a passing accuracy test.
- Highly concentrated routing is not universally faster: a separate cold-L2 experiment showed about 7.6% regression for FC1 alone with one active expert, despite a small combined FC1+FC2 gain.
- Only H20 EP8 was validated. EP1/EP2 deployments, H100/H200, broad model quality parity and matched source-serving A/B are not claimed; a paired 500-item GSM8K sanity check is reported above.

Related but distinct:

- #57772 requests a fused SM90 MegaMoE path; this report concerns dispatch in the existing converted block-FP8 CUTLASS MoE path.
- #57423 / #57635 concern FlashInfer autotune cache restart deadlock, not this dispatch estimate.

AI assistance was used for diagnosis, implementation, validation and preparation of this report.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Relevant recorded environment (not a fresh full `collect_env.py` dump):

```text
GPU: single node, 8 x NVIDIA H20, SM90, 78 SM/GPU, 97,871 MiB/GPU
vLLM: 0.30.0
Image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0 (registry mirror)
Image digest: sha256:8a69ffad015f138d7170c4ddc429e230a3bc1c1719f67e14324749df200a4b90
FlashInfer: 0.6.18.post1
PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA runtime: 13.0
Serving model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, converted FP8 expert/non-expert weights
Weight block size: 128 x 128
Serving parallelism: TP8, EP8, DP1
MoE backend: flashinfer_cutlass
Main operator geometry: hidden=5120, intermediate=2304, top-k=6
Physical experts: 384 routed experts + 16 EPLB replicas = 400, 50/rank
Draft operator geometry: 128 physical experts, 16/rank, top-k=3
```

### Before submitting a new issue...

- Searched existing open/closed issues for `expected_m`, SM90 FP8 dispatch, H20 FlashInfer MoE performance and the upstream PR link; no matching root-cause report was found.
- Documentation chatbot was not consulted; this report is based on source-level diagnosis and measured operator A/B, rather than a configuration question.

title: [RFC]: Expert-granular MoE residency — drive UVA offload from EPLB's per-expert load statistics
body:
### Motivation.

vLLM can already offload MoE expert weights to host memory, and it already knows which experts are hot. It cannot yet use the second fact to drive the first.

What exists on `main` today:

* `PrefetchOffloadConfig.offload_group_size` / `offload_num_in_group` — choose **which layers** to offload.
* `UVAOffloadConfig.cpu_offload_params` — choose **which parameters** to offload, by name segment. Its own docstring uses `"mlp.experts.w2_weight"` as the example.
* `offload_backend="uva"`, with `is_uva_available()` and `get_accelerator_view_from_cpu_tensor()` — zero-copy access to pinned host memory.
* `EPLBConfig.window_size` / `step_interval` and EPLB's `expert_load_window` — a rolling record of **observed per-expert load**, already used to periodically rearrange expert *placement* across ranks.

The gap is that `cpu_offload_params` matches whole tensors. It moves `w2_weight` for *all* experts in a layer, or none of them. There is no way to express "this fraction of experts is cold under current traffic; demote them and keep the rest resident", even though the statistics that identify them are already being collected, and the cadence for acting on them already exists.

For a wide-MoE model this is the difference between offload being unusable and being the thing that makes the model fit. Expert weights dominate, routing is heavily skewed in practice, and the cold tail is large and fairly stable over a window. Offloading whole expert tensors costs far too much; offloading the cold tail costs comparatively little and frees VRAM that is worth more as KV cache.

### Proposed Change.

Reuse EPLB's existing loop. It already answers "which experts are cold" and "when do we act on that". This proposal adds only "and therefore where does each expert live".

**1. A fraction, not a count.** One knob:

```
cold_expert_fraction: float = 0.0   # 0.0 disables; e.g. 0.15
```

Per layer, `n_cold = floor(num_local_experts * cold_expert_fraction)`, so it is model- and TP-independent. A raw count is deliberately not offered — it does not transfer across models, and it is the kind of number that ends up hardcoded in a deployment and silently wrong after a reshard.

**2. Residency derived from the load window, on the existing cadence.** At each EPLB rebalance step, rank experts by `expert_load_window` and mark the coldest `n_cold` per layer as host-resident; the rest stay device-resident. This is deliberately the *same* trigger and the *same* data EPLB already uses to rearrange placement — residency rebalance alongside placement rebalance, not a second scheduler.

Between rebalance steps the split is **static**. That is the point; see rejected alternatives.

**3. A two-bank forward.** Run the stock expert forward once over the device bank and once over the host bank, and sum. Two `expert_map`s. Router top-k computed once and reused. Shared experts added on the device call only, so they are not double-counted.

**4. Correct split ordering.** The split must happen *after* `process_weights_after_loading`, because the weights must already carry the quant method's real repacked layout. The kernel/config must be rebuilt for **both** banks — one config shared across two banks silently runs cold weights against hot scales, which does not crash and produces plausible wrong output. This was a real bug we hit.

**5. The ranking policy is a hook.** `expert_load_window` is the default input, but the selection itself should be pluggable so deployments can substitute their own signal. I am not proposing to upstream a particular ranker.

### Rejected alternatives.

**Per-token swap-on-demand with prefetch.** The obvious design — keep a small resident cache and fetch an expert from host when a token routes to it — does not work, and it is worth writing down why so nobody re-derives it.

MoE routing is data-dependent. The expert set for layer *L* is known only after computing layer *L*'s router logits, which requires layer *L−1*'s output. There is no lookahead window to prefetch into: by the time the requirement is known, the weights are needed immediately, on the critical path.

The cost, from our measurements (1 × H100 80 GB, 2.53 MB per expert per layer, 48 layers, 10 active experts/token):

| | |
|---|---|
| all-resident decode | 45.7 tok/s → 21.9 ms/token → ~456 µs/layer |
| measured host gather, one cold expert | 63.2 µs = **14% of one layer's budget** |
| if one of ten active experts per layer is cold | +3.0 ms/token → decode falls to ~40 tok/s |

And that is for a *single* cold expert per layer. Swapping also means mutating the device bank during inference, which invalidates CUDA-graph captures and changes `expert_map` in flight.

Periodic re-derivation gets the adaptivity without any of this: the transfer cost is paid once per rebalance interval rather than once per token, which amortizes it to nothing.

**Tiered hot/warm/cold with threshold rules.** Considered and dropped. We cannot justify specific tier thresholds with the data we have, and a fraction plus a pluggable policy spans the same space with one parameter instead of several.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### Any Other Things.

**The honest version of our measurements.**

Setup: 1 × H100 80 GB, a 48-layer MoE with 512 experts/layer and 10 active per token, 88 experts offloaded per layer (17.2%, the static equivalent of `cold_expert_fraction=0.17`). The checkpoint is assembled (compressed-tensors INT4 body with an FP8 embedding), not a published one — so these numbers are **not independently reproducible**, which is a real limitation of this evidence.

| | all resident | 88/512 offloaded |
|---|---|---|
| model memory at load | 68.18 GiB | 58.52 GiB (−9.66 GiB) |
| GPU KV cache | 144,725 tok | 522,878 tok |
| decode @ concurrency 1 | 45.7 tok/s | 37.1 tok/s (−19%) |
| latency @ concurrency 4 | 7.65 s | 3.67 s |

Four caveats a reviewer should have up front:

1. **The concurrency-4 improvement is not cheaper compute.** It is the larger KV pool avoiding preemption: `num_preemptions_total` went 0 → 3 in the all-resident run and stayed 0 throughout the offloaded one. Offload does not make decode faster; it stopped the scheduler thrashing.

2. **The cold-expert cost is 2–4× what the naive model predicts, and I cannot explain it.** Naive estimate 1.15–2.15 ms/token at the measured cold-hit fraction; observed ≈5.1 ms/token at concurrency 1. Unverified candidates: PCIe contention with other host-resident tensors streaming each step, ~48 extra kernel launches per decode step, hot-bank geometry change. **This is the single biggest open question** and the main thing I would want help with. EPLB's per-expert counters look like the right instrument for attacking it.

3. **Only 0 and 88 offloaded experts have ever been latency-measured.** Every other fraction is extrapolation sitting on top of the gap in (2).

4. **9.66 GiB is measured at load; the arithmetic prediction was 9.97 GiB.** The 3.1% gap is real and unexplained.

Net: the memory saving is solid and the KV headroom it buys is large. The latency story is workload-dependent — a loss at low concurrency, a win at higher concurrency for tail-heavy traffic — and it rests on a cost model that does not yet close. I would rather agree the shape here before re-implementing a ~600-line change to the MoE forward path against a tree that has since been restructured.

Two adjacent findings from the same work, filed separately as PRs: #57792 and #57793.

title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
body:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

title: [Bug]: No sm_121 (Blackwell) support on aarch64 — NVIDIA DGX Spark / Acer GN100
body:
### Your current environment
**System Info** - GPU: NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip (sm_121) - Architecture: aarch64 (ARM v9.2-A) - CUDA: 13.0 - OS: NVIDIA DGX OS (Ubuntu 24.04 base) - RAM: 128 GB LPDDR5x unified memory (CPU + GPU shared pool) - Device: NVIDIA DGX Spark / Acer Veriton GN100 - vLLM image tested: avarok/vllm-dgx-spark:v11 **Describe the issue** vLLM fails to start on NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10 Blackwell, sm_121) because the bundled PyTorch binary only includes compiled CUDA kernels through sm_120. The GPU is detected but no compatible kernels exist for the actual compute capability. This is a build-time issue — the shipped .so files lack sm_121 targets. Runtime workarounds (TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST, LD_LIBRARY_PATH compat libs) have no effect on prebuilt binaries. **Error behavior** vLLM crashes at startup during CUDA kernel initialization. PyTorch reports supported architectures up to sm_120 but the GPU requires sm_121. **Expected behavior** vLLM should support sm_121 (Blackwell) on aarch64, either via: 1. Official PyTorch wheels built with sm_121 + aarch64 targets 2. vLLM Docker images compiled against sm_121-capable PyTorch 3. Documentation of the supported build path for DGX Spark users **Context** The NVIDIA DGX Spark (and its OEM variant Acer Veriton GN100) is shipping to customers now. It is an ARM64-only device with 128 GB unified memory and sm_121 Blackwell GPU. This is becoming a common edge AI inference platform. Currently the only working local LLM serving option on this hardware is Ollama (which ships its own llama.cpp backend with Blackwell support). **Workaround** Use Ollama for inference. vLLM is not functional on this hardware with any available container image. **Additional context** - PyTorch nightly may have sm_121 support but no official aarch64 + cu130 wheels are published yet - NVIDIA NIM containers may work but are model-limited and require enterprise licensing - Community image avarok/vllm-dgx-spark:v11 was the closest attempt but its PyTorch build stops at sm_120 The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug vLLM's prebuilt container ships PyTorch binaries compiled with CUDA kernels for GPU architectures up to sm_120. The DGX Spark's Blackwell GPU requires sm_121. Since there are no matching kernels in the binary, vLLM crashes at startup. It's a compile-time gap — the fix has to come from rebuilding PyTorch and vLLM with sm_121 targets, not from runtime configuration. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Bug]: Responses API `truncation: "auto"` truncates at the token level from the left, dropping `instructions` first and cutting mid-item
body:
### Your current environment

vLLM `main` (also affects the pending Harmony fixes #38143 / #39413). The field exists but was a no-op in v0.15.1.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`truncation: "auto"` on `/v1/responses` is implemented by mapping the request to
`truncate_prompt_tokens=-1`:

- `vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/serving.py` (main), inside `get_max_tokens(...)`:
  `truncate_prompt_tokens=(-1 if request.truncation != "disabled" else None)` — appears twice (initial request and the built-in-tools loop).
- `-1` resolves to `max_model_len` in `vllm/entrypoints/utils.py::_validate_truncation_size`, and the prompt is then cut to the **last** N tokens of the fully rendered prompt (`SamplingParams.truncate_prompt_tokens` docstring: "will use only the last k tokens from the prompt (i.e., left truncation)").

That differs from the OpenAI spec this field is meant to mirror (`openai-python`, `response_create_params.py`):

> `auto`: If the input to this Response exceeds the model's context window size, the model will truncate the response to fit the context window by **dropping items from the beginning of the conversation**.

Two consequences of the current implementation:

1. **`instructions` is discarded first.** `instructions` is a top-level parameter, not an input item, so under the spec it is never dropped. In vLLM it is rendered as the system/developer message at the head of the token sequence, so it is the first thing a left cut removes. The model then answers with no instructions while the response object still reports `truncation: "auto"`.
2. **Truncation is not item-aligned.** The cut can land in the middle of a message, or in the middle of the chat-template header, leaving the model a prompt that starts with half a message and stray template tokens.

### Expected behavior

Match the spec: drop whole items from the front of `input` until the rendered prompt fits `max_model_len - max_output_tokens`, keep `instructions` (and the final user item) intact, and never split an item. If a single item is itself too large to fit, return the existing 400 rather than silently truncating inside it.

### Suggested fix

Implement `auto` at the item level in the Responses serving path before rendering (iteratively drop `input[0]`, re-render, re-count), and stop passing `truncate_prompt_tokens=-1` for this mode. #38143 / #39413 could adopt the same helper for the Harmony path instead of adding a second token-level left cut.

### Related

- #38132 (original report; closed as stale)
- #38143, #39413 (pending Harmony fixes, both token-level left truncation)
- #37011 (structured `context_length_exceeded` error code; would help clients that opt to handle truncation themselves)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On `/v1/responses`, `truncation: "auto"` is implemented as token-level left truncation of the fully rendered prompt (`truncate_prompt_tokens=-1`), not as the item-level "drop items from the beginning of the conversation" the OpenAI spec describes. Two visible effects:

1. `instructions` is dropped first. It is rendered as the system message at the head of the token sequence, so a left cut removes it before any input item, even though the spec treats `instructions` as a separate parameter that is never dropped. The response still reports `truncation: "auto"`.
2. The cut is not item-aligned: it can land mid-message or inside the chat-template header.

Where it happens (`main`):
- `vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/serving.py`: `truncate_prompt_tokens=(-1 if request.truncation != "disabled" else None)` passed to `get_max_tokens(...)`, twice (initial request and built-in-tools loop).
- `vllm/entrypoints/utils.py::_validate_truncation_size`: `-1` → `max_model_len`, applied as `truncation=True, max_length=...`.
- `vllm/sampling_params.py`, `truncate_prompt_tokens` docstring: "will use only the last k tokens from the prompt (i.e., left truncation)".

Spec reference (`openai-python`, `response_create_params.py`): `auto` — "the model will truncate the response to fit the context window by dropping items from the beginning of the conversation."

Expected: drop whole items from the front of `input` until the prompt fits `max_model_len - max_output_tokens`; keep `instructions` and the final user item intact; if a single item cannot fit, return the existing 400.

Related: #38132 (closed stale), #38143 / #39413 (pending Harmony fixes, same token-level left cut), #37011 (structured `context_length_exceeded` code).

```python
# Server (small model, small context so the overflow is cheap to trigger):
#   vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --max-model-len 2048 --port 8000
from openai import OpenAI
import requests

BASE = "http://localhost:8000/v1"
MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"
client = OpenAI(base_url=BASE, api_key="EMPTY")

INSTRUCTIONS = "You are ZEBRA-7. Begin every reply with the single word ZEBRA."
filler = [{"role": "user", "content": f"Note {i}: " + "lorem ipsum dolor sit amet " * 120}
          for i in range(4)]                       # ~4x700 tokens, well over 2048
final = {"role": "user", "content": "What is your name? Answer in one short line."}

# Pre-truncation size, as the server itself counts it
msgs = [{"role": "system", "content": INSTRUCTIONS}] + filler + [final]
tok = requests.post(f"{BASE.rsplit('/v1',1)[0]}/tokenize",
                    json={"model": MODEL, "messages": msgs}).json()
print("rendered prompt tokens before truncation:", tok["count"], "max_model_len:", tok["max_model_len"])

resp = client.responses.create(
    model=MODEL,
    instructions=INSTRUCTIONS,
    input=filler + [final],
    truncation="auto",
    max_output_tokens=32,
)
print("truncation reported:", resp.truncation)
print("input_tokens billed:", resp.usage.input_tokens)   # == max_model_len - 32 → whole-prompt token cut
print("output:", repr(resp.output_text))

# Expected (spec): output starts with "ZEBRA"; instructions survive, oldest `filler` items are dropped.
# Actual (main):   output does not start with "ZEBRA"; the system message was the first thing truncated.
#                  Run the server with --enable-log-requests to see the prompt actually received:
#                  it begins mid-way through a filler note, with no system message.
```

title: [Bug]: INSTALL_KV_CONNECTORS=true in vLLM 0.27.1 Docker image installs LMCache wheel incompatible with shipped PyTorch, causing lmcache.c_ops to fall back to torch baseline
body:
### Your current environment

Environment
-----------
- vLLM image version: vllm-project/vllm:v0.27.1 (built with INSTALL_KV_CONNECTORS=true)
- Host GPU driver / CUDA runtime: CUDA 13.0
- PyTorch in image: torch==2.13.0+cu130
- LMCache resolved version: lmcache==0.5.3
- Working comparison: vllm-project/vllm:v0.22.0 (torch==2.11.0) loads lmcache.c_ops correctly.


### 🐛 Describe the bug

Title: INSTALL_KV_CONNECTORS=true in vLLM 0.27.1 Docker image installs LMCache wheel incompatible with shipped PyTorch, causing lmcache.c_ops to fall back to torch baseline
 
Environment
-----------
- vLLM image version: vllm-project/vllm:v0.27.1 (built with INSTALL_KV_CONNECTORS=true)
- Host GPU driver / CUDA runtime: CUDA 13.0
- PyTorch in image: torch==2.13.0+cu130
- LMCache resolved version: lmcache==0.5.3
- Working comparison: vllm-project/vllm:v0.22.0 (torch==2.11.0) loads lmcache.c_ops correctly.
 
Reproduction
------------
Build the official image:
 
    docker build -t vllm:0.27.1-lmcache \
      --build-arg INSTALL_KV_CONNECTORS=true \
      -f docker/Dockerfile .
 
Deploy any model with kv_connector="LMCacheConnectorV1" or LMCacheMPConnector, then inspect the vLLM pod logs.
 
Observed behavior
-----------------
vLLM 0.27.1 logs:
 
    [LMCache WARNING] lmcache.c_ops compiled extension not found; CudaDeviceOps stays on the torch baseline for all ops.
    [LMCache INFO] multi_layer_block_kv_transfer mode: tensor
 
vLLM 0.22.0 logs:
 
    [LMCache INFO] multi_layer_block_kv_transfer mode: ptr
 
Root cause
----------
requirements/kv_connectors.txt currently pins:
 
    lmcache >= 0.3.9
 
and docker/Dockerfile installs it with:
 
    uv pip install --system -r /tmp/kv_connectors.txt --no-build || ( ...source build fallback... )
 
The first --no-build path installs the LMCache wheel from PyPI. That wheel is compiled against torch==2.11.0 (matching LMCache/pyproject.toml's build-system pin), but vLLM 0.27.1 ships torch==2.13.0. The compiled lmcache.c_ops extension fails to import at runtime due to PyTorch C++ ABI mismatch.
 
Because the wheel install itself succeeds, the Dockerfile's source-build fallback is never executed, so the extension is never recompiled against the vLLM image's actual torch version.
 
vLLM 0.22.0 works only because it also ships torch==2.11.0, which happens to match the LMCache wheel's ABI.
 
Suggested fixes
---------------
1. Force source build against the image's torch
   In the connector install step, build LMCache from source so c_ops is compiled against the same PyTorch/CUDA versions vLLM ships, e.g.:
 
       uv pip install --system -r /tmp/kv_connectors.txt --no-build-isolation --no-binary :lmcache:
 
2. Pin a torch-ABI-compatible LMCache version/wheel
   Update requirements/kv_connectors.txt to reference a lmcache wheel or version built against torch==2.13.0.
 
3. Upstream LMCache wheel matrix
   Coordinate with LMCache to publish wheels for each supported PyTorch ABI, similar to other torch extensions.
 
Expected behavior
-----------------
When INSTALL_KV_CONNECTORS=true is used, the resulting image should load lmcache.c_ops successfully and log:
 
    multi_layer_block_kv_transfer mode: ptr
 
regardless of the vLLM release's PyTorch version.
 
Impact
------
Without lmcache.c_ops, LMCache falls back to the torch baseline path for KV cache transfer. This can silently degrade performance for users who expect the optimized native CUDA path, especially with disaggregated prefill / CPU offloading scenarios.
